newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhs determined to end oil sell-offs by July 1.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhs determined to end oil sell-offs by July 1.

text.p: Kazakhstan is determined to sell off its massive, and potentially lucrative oil industry to strategic investors by the end of next month despite resistance from enterprise managers, a senior minister said on Monday.

"I think the target set by the president -- to finalise... the privatisation of the oil and gas sector by July 1 this year -- will be fulfilled in time," Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference on Monday.
"Of course, we mean by this the attraction of strategic investors," said Eduard Utepov, who is in charge of the finance ministry's privatisation department.
Shares left over after stakes are sold to strategic investors will be floated on the new Kazakh stockmarket which is to be set up by the end of the year, officials say.

Proving its determination to go ahead with sell-offs of the former Soviet republic's troubled but promising oil companies, the government on Sunday struck a deal with Indonesia's Central Asia Petroleum Ltd, which got a 60-percent stake in Kazakhstan's largest oil company Mangistaumunaigaz.

Central Asia Petroleum purchased the stake for a total of $4.348 billion. Within the next 20 years the company must invest $4.1 billion, including $2 billion in the first five years. It will pay the government a $248 million bonus.
The Indonesian partner says its investment will help double the output of Mangistaumunaigaz within the first five years.

The decay of Mangistaumunaigaz, which sits on estimated reserves of 200 million tonnes but whose production fell to just four million tonnes a year from 25 million tonnes in Soviet times, is typical for Kazakhstan's oil industry.

But government attempts to attract a massive influx of foreign capital and revive the potentially wealthy oil industry are thwarted by the resistance of the Central Asian state's oil barons, who have headed oil enterprises since Soviet times.

In the case of Mangistaumunaigaz, management wanted its shares to be traded on international markets rather than sold directly to investors, but the government rejected this because the company had not been audited by a Western company and had not passed through Kazakh listing procedures.
"When we talk about selling a large company like Mangistaumunaigaz, there will always be the collision...of interests of different groups and representatives of various clans," Pavlov said.
But despite this resistance the government would continue sell-offs, Pavlov said.
On Tuesday the tender committee will decide the winner of the tender for the right to own an 85 percent stake in Aktyubinskmunaigaz oil company in Kazakhstan's north-west.
"Some two or three days later, we will consider bids for the development of the Uzen oilfield," Pavlov said.

Officials say the Uzenmunaigaz enterprise, in southwest Kazakhstan near the Caspian Sea, sits on estimated oil reserves of 852 million tonnes -- the second largest in the country after the Tengiz oil field.

U.S. Chevron Corp and Mobil Corp are already developing Kazakhstan's Tengiz, the largest oilfield to be discovered in the world in the last 20 years. Tengiz has estimated reserves of at least one billion tonnes and peak output is targeted at 30-35 million tonnes a year.

Nurlan Balgimbayev, head of the recently formed state Kazakh Oil company, has said Kazakhstan was planning to become the world's sixth largest oil producer by the year 2010, boosting output to 170 million tonnes from 26.5 million this year.
Foreign companies have so far invested in Kazakhstan's oil sector over $2 billion, he said.
